raw_record.support_text: In patients treated for macrolide-resistant Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, drug-related adverse events were assessed for multidrug regimens that included rifabutin, ethambutol, ethionamide, streptomycin, amikacin, ciprofloxacin, clofazimine, linezolid, and rifampin. The authors explicitly state that no patients experienced significant hepatotoxicity with any of the agents used.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Multidrug regimens for macrolide-resistant MAC lung disease begun after resistance was recognized; drug toxicity data record significant symptoms or adverse events requiring dosage change or discontinuation; reported incidence likely underestimates true toxicity because not all patients were monitored at UTHCT for the full duration of therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 10% (4/40) of ethambutol-treated patients experienced ocular toxicity, but no significant hepatotoxicity was reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a long-term analysis continuing a US study of donepezil, 133 patients completed a trial lasting nearly 5 years; adverse events were reported as mild and transient, and there was no evidence of liver toxicity. This is an explicit negative conclusion that donepezil does not cause liver injury in human therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Explicit negative: 'no evidence of liver toxicity' in a ~5-year continuation analysis of the US study (133 completers). Also, the paper credits donepezil, a piperidine-based compound, with a 'lack of liver side effects' compared with other cholinesterase inhibitors; its adverse effects were mostly digestive (diarrhea, nausea, vomiting) consistent with cholinergic action, not hepatic. Data from randomized trials in probable Alzheimer's disease (818 patients in a multinational study at 5 and 10 mg/day; US study; 12-month Nordic study; 24-week severe AD study).

raw_record.support_text: In this randomized dose-ranging trial of rosuvastatin (1-80 mg) versus placebo and atorvastatin in patients with hyperlipidemia, no clinically significant elevations in ALT, aspartate aminotransferase, or creatine kinase were observed during treatment in any patient, providing an explicit statement that no clinically significant liver enzyme (and thus DILI-related) changes were attributed to rosuvastatin in this human clinical trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized dose-ranging trial of rosuvastatin 1-80 mg versus placebo and atorvastatin; no clinically significant ALT, aspartate aminotransferase, or creatine kinase elevations observed in any patient. Most common treatment-related adverse events in rosuvastatin groups were nausea, diarrhea, dry mouth, and abdominal pain; no myopathy cases reported.

raw_record.support_text: Piperaquine data were examined because piperaquine has no known DILI risk, despite extensive use in acute uncomplicated malaria. In Study QP15C01, ALT/AST elevations observed in 3/8 participants after piperaquine administration were attributed to parasitemia reduction by an effective antimalarial drug and to participant susceptibility/recrudescence, rather than to piperaquine-induced liver injury, leading to early study termination before a planned repeat cipargamin dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Context is a controlled induced blood stage malaria (IBSM) volunteer model. Liver-enzyme elevations seen in this setting were attributed to malaria/parasitemia and co-medications, not to piperaquine; the paper explicitly states piperaquine has no known DILI risk (reference 10). In QP15C05 2/12 participants showed ALT/AST elevations (R109 4.2 x ULN, R110 9.2 x ULN) after 480 mg piperaquine on day 8; QP13C05 showed one moderate ALT increase (R019 3.7 x ULN); QP14C21 showed none, with earlier treatment (day 7) and lower inoculum (1,800 parasites) appearing protective.

raw_record.support_text: This study of almost 5 million antidepressant initiators found no evidence of an increased risk of serious liver injury associated with 'other antidepressants' including mianserin when compared with SSRIs in real-life settings, representing an explicit negative causal conclusion for human DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Comparison group was SSRI users; finding applies to real-life settings.
raw_record.extra_details: Pharmacoepidemiologic cohort of nearly 5 million antidepressant initiators; outcome was serious liver injury causing hospitalization or death, identified via ICD-10 codes.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of fifty patients anesthetized with methoxyflurane, nitrous oxide and oxygen (induction shortened by thiopentone), the serum transaminase levels measured before and after anesthesia were taken to indicate that methoxyflurane is atoxic for the liver (methoxyflurane is not hepatotoxic). This is an explicit agent-specific negative conclusion about methoxyflurane-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Fifty patients received methoxyflurane, nitrous oxide (protoxyde d'azote) and oxygen anesthesia, with thiopentone for induction. Serum transaminase levels before and after anesthesia did not indicate liver damage, leading the authors to conclude methoxyflurane is atoxic to the liver. Other observations: frequent hypotension often unrelated to anesthetic depth, bradycardia, respiratory depression, good muscle relaxation, reduced bleeding, increased glycemia during and after surgery, reduced postoperative analgesic needs, frequent postoperative nausea and vomiting, and delayed recovery of consciousness.

raw_record.extra_details: 41% (18/44) of rifabutin-treated patients had gastrointestinal symptoms or polymyalgia/polyarthralgia syndrome, but no significant hepatotoxicity was reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase I study of TAC-101 in 29 patients with advanced solid tumors, hepatic transaminase (ALT) elevations were frequently observed at grade 1, and grade 2 ALT increases occurred in two of 28 patients (7%). The authors explicitly state that there was no dose-limiting hepatotoxicity observed with TAC-101 administration, concluding that TAC-101 did not cause dose-limiting hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I clinical trial in 29 patients with advanced solid tumors (bronchogenic, head and neck, sarcoma, prostate, colorectal, thymoma, pleural mesothelioma). Hepatic transaminase (ALT) elevations were frequently observed at grade 1 (NCI CTC v2.0) with grade 2 ALT increases in 2/28 patients (7%). LDH elevations (>50% above baseline) in 22/29 patients; no changes in vitamin A, LH, FSH, or testosterone. Authors concluded no dose-limiting hepatotoxicity was observed.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion concludes that a toxic hepatitis occurred twice in this patient after ingestion of psoralen (methoxsalen) during PUVA therapy. The rapid onset of symptoms 4-5 hours after methoxsalen ingestion on treatment days and rapid defervescence and resolution of liver enzymes with symptomatic therapy strongly suggest a toxic drug reaction rather than a viral origin or extrahepatic biliary pathology; a viral origin was considered unlikely due to negative HAA testing and repetition of the reaction after readministration of methoxsalen, and other medications were excluded because they were continued without recurrence.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient with psoriasis undergoing PUVA photochemotherapy; after a scheduled PUVA treatment she ingested 50 mg oral methoxsalen and received UVA (4 joules) 2 hours later. Four hours after ingestion temperature rose to 39.5 C, LDH to 905, SGOT to 870, and alkaline phosphatase to 111; she defervesced within 24 h and enzymes returned to normal over 5 days. HAA was negative; intravenous cholangiogram unsuccessful because liver function was too poor to excrete dye; no liver biopsy. The reaction recurred after repeat methoxsalen readministration (rechallenge), supporting causality. The same patient later used topical methoxsalen with no similar reaction. Note: the discussion heading refers to 'methotrexate-induced toxic hepatitis,' but the attributed administered causal agent throughout is methoxsalen (psoralen).

raw_record.support_text: The initial diagnosis in this case report was a drug reaction secondary to diphenylhydantoin (phenytoin), which was therefore discontinued. The patient's liver injury was evidenced by centrilobular necrosis on biopsy (with patchy leukocyte infiltration), elevated serum bilirubin (1.55 mg/100 ml, mostly conjugated) and SGOT of 180 units, and he recovered after treatment with prednisone.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper records diphenylhydantoin (phenytoin) under its synonym 'diphenylhydantoin'. Case presented as a severe toxic/drug reaction; liver histology showed centrilobular necrosis with patchy leukocyte infiltration (H&E), and follow-up biopsy after 9 days of steroid therapy showed near-complete regeneration with residual scarring. Labs: serum bilirubin 1.55 mg/100 ml (1.10 conjugated, 0.45 unconjugated), SGOT 180 units, alkaline phosphatase 2.95 Bessie-Lowry units, prothrombin time 15 sec (control 13 sec), total protein 6.5 G/100 ml with albumin 2.9 G. Diphenylhydantoin was discontinued and the reaction was treated symptomatically with acetylsalicylic acid; prednisone (30 mg/day increased to 60 mg/day) was started on hospital day 3; patient became afebrile and asymptomatic by hospital day 5. Acetylsalicylic acid and prednisone were given to treat the reaction and are not attributed as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of ramipril-induced liver injury proven by positive rechallenge, and (per the RUCAM assessment) the case was classified as 'highly probable' with a score of 12 of 15. The patient presented with jaundice and highly elevated ALT and ALP (mixed pattern), developing 10 months after starting ramipril, with normalization after rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: First ramipril DILI case proven by positive rechallenge; RUCAM score 12/15 ('highly probable'); time to onset 10 months; presented with jaundice and highly elevated ALT and ALP; outcome was normalization after dechallenge/rechallenge. Pattern expected to include cholestasis but hepatocellular damage also possible.

raw_record.support_text: In an open trial of stanozolol (10 mg daily, anabolic steroid with fibrinolytic-enhancing activity) for severe post-surgical low-back pain, many patients withdrew from a larger initial cohort because of toxic side-effects attributed to the treatment, including weight gain, hypertension, hepatotoxicity, acneiform rash, and hirsutism with voice changes in females. Only the 18 patients completing at least 12 months of therapy were included in the analysis; all had normal hepatic biochemical profiles prior to treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Open trial, stanozolol 10 mg daily for severe back and radicular pain after lumbar disc surgery. Hepatotoxicity was one of several toxic side-effects (along with weight gain, hypertension, acneiform rash, hirsutism, voice changes in females) causing withdrawal from the initially recruited larger cohort; only the 18 completers (at least 12 months therapy) were analyzed. No pre-existing hepatic disease; all had normal plasma hepatic profiles before treatment. Hepatotoxicity was not further characterized (no phenotype, severity, or case count reported).

raw_record.support_text: In an in vitro MPCC case study, fialuridine, a nucleoside analog drug for hepatitis B viral infection, caused the deaths of 5 patients in clinical trials due to lactic acidosis, a drastic human DILI outcome not predicted previously by rat, dog, or monkey studies. The paper notes that such human DILI was not previously predicted in those animal models.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analog drug for hepatitis B viral infection; caused deaths of 5 patients in clinical trials due to lactic acidosis; this human DILI outcome was not predicted by prior rat, dog, or monkey in vivo studies; in human MPCCs dosing for 4-21 days produced dose- and time-dependent toxicity (mitochondrial activity, albumin, urea, morphological alterations).

raw_record.support_text: After withdrawal from phenprocoumon therapy and switching to low molecular weight heparin, liver tests gradually normalized; aminotransferase levels rapidly increased again when phenprocoumon was resumed. Phenprocoumon-associated necrotizing hepatitis was diagnosed by clinical course, liver histology (necrotizing hepatocellular injury in zone 3 of the acinus) and a positive lymphocyte transformation test, and liver enzymes normalized after restart of prednisolone. The authors conclude that, though severe hepatic adverse effects of phenprocoumon are rare, physicians should consider coumarin derivatives as a potential source of hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case in a 52-year-old female on anticoagulation after aortic valve replacement due to aortic stenosis. Latency about 7 months between start of anticoagulation and disease manifestation; serological tests for viral, autoimmune and metabolic hepatitis were negative; first lymphocyte transformation test with phenprocoumon was negative, a repeat test one week later was positive. Rechallenge on resuming phenprocoumon produced rapid rises in aminotransferases; dechallenge (switch to low molecular weight heparin) led to gradual normalization; prednisolone immunosuppression was restarted before recovery. The authors note severe hepatic adverse effects of phenprocoumon are rare.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the case of a 44-year-old woman with chronic paranoid schizophrenia given clozapine, 400 mg/day, as monotherapy. During the fifth week of treatment her previously unremarkable transaminase levels dramatically rose to 675 U/liter for ALT and 369 U/liter for AST, with only a slight increase in gamma-glutamyltransferase (67 U/liter) and unremarkable bilirubin and cholestatic parameters; she developed 28% eosinophilia, and serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were negative. This case is presented as toxic hepatitis caused by clozapine treatment in a letter titled 'Toxic Hepatitis by Clozapine Treatment'. A previously reported clozapine case of toxic hepatitis accompanied by jaundice and bone marrow damage showed enzymes increased to 133 (ALT) and 268 (AST) U/liter.
raw_record.extra_details: Clozapine given at 400 mg/day as monotherapy; toxic hepatitis developed during the fifth week of treatment. ALT 675 U/liter, AST 369 U/liter, gamma-glutamyltransferase 67 U/liter; bilirubin and other cholestatic parameters unremarkable; 28% eosinophilia; negative serology for hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus; testing for autoimmune-chronic-active-hepatitis autoantibodies reported. Named phenotype 'toxic hepatitis' with eosinophilia. A prior published clozapine case described toxic hepatitis with jaundice and bone marrow damage (ALT 133, AST 268 U/liter). Background: transient moderate asymptomatic transaminase increases in about 50% of clozapine-treated patients (mean ALT 55, max 172 U/liter; mean AST 34, max 96 U/liter) have been suggested to be an adaptive reaction, but this is not presented as DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A second case of toxic hepatitis with ketoconazole is reported: a 48-year-old physician treated for fingernail onychomycosis with ketoconazole 200 mg/day orally developed fatigue, nausea, icterus, and marked elevation of ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase after about 81 days of therapy, with viral hepatitis A and B excluded and no history of liver disease or other medications. A single extra 200 mg ketoconazole dose 48 hours before day 86 testing further accelerated the rise; findings returned to normal within 2 months of drug cessation. The letter also cites a prior biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis case with ketoconazole and the manufacturer's advisory reporting the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: fingernail onychomycosis (open multicenter study), unresponsive previously to griseofulvin. Dose: single oral 200 mg daily. Hepatitis onset after ~81 days of therapy; fatigue and nausea at ~day 78 leading to cessation. Laboratory: AST 1030 U/L on day 84 rising to 1900 U/L on day 86 (normal 10-40); total bilirubin 107-111 µmol/L (normal 2-17); alkaline phosphatase 450-480 U/L (normal 50-275); LDH 600-800 U/L (normal 150-450); icterus and marked malaise. Viral hepatitis A and B excluded; liver/pancreas ultrasound and CT normal; patient refused biopsy. Rechallenge-like acceleration after a single 200 mg dose 48h before day 86. Recovery to normal within 2 months after stopping. Prior communication reported a biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis case with ketoconazole; manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reported the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy. Estimated ~300,000 prescriptions since licensing in the US in 1981.
